node.title: Re: Reading a hash structure stored in a file
node.author: haukex
node.doctext:
The main problem is that [doc://my] declares a lexical variable, meaning it is restricted to its lexical scope. [doc://eval]ed code has its own lexical scope, so the surrounding code can't see the %hash1 declared inside the [doc://eval]ed code. One possible way to fix this issue would be to append some code to the string that you are [doc://eval]ing that returns the values, so for example something like my $hash1ref = eval($code."; return \\%hash1;");

However, [doc://eval] will execute arbitrary code, and if you use it for untrusted code, it might allow an attacker to inject any code into your system, which is of course a bad thing. One possible way around this is with my module [mod://Config::Perl], which will parse data structures like the one you showed. For example:

use warnings; use strict; use Config::Perl; use Data::Dumper; my $parser = Config::Perl->new; my $data = $parser->parse_or_die('file.pl'); my %hash1 = %{ $data->{'%hash1'} }; print Dumper(\%hash1); __END__ $VAR1 = { 'hi' => 2, 'hello' => 1 };

Another issue with your original code is that you need to give [doc://eval] a string, not a filehandle. A simple way to slurp a file into memory is my $code = do { local $/; <$fh> };. Also, if you really want to use [doc://eval], you should check it for errors, in the above example by checking if $hash1ref is [doc://defined] or not. Update: Also, instead of [doc://eval]ing a file, there's [doc://do]. But as I said, I wouldn't recommend these methods.
